CovalentFormer · v4b

CovalentFormer — A Covalent Medicinal Chemist Assistant

Qwen2.5-7B + LoRA over 585,530 rows — reaction chemistry, analogue design, and pocket-conditioned covalent hit-to-lead — with a Siamese ΔpIC50 head.

2026-10-03

GLU166unmet carboxylate in S3OE2 is 4.56 Å from the nearest ligand N/OGrow a short donor off the P3 arm — one bond-length turns a near-miss into the canonical S3 hydrogen bond.
HIS163S1 anchor left unusedND1 4.70 Å from any ligand N/O, though the hit already carries a pyrrolidinoneReach it: shorten or re-angle the P1 arm so the lactam carbonyl meets ND1 — the move the shortened-linker lead makes.
ASN142 / SER144polar rim facing a carbonOD1 3.24 Å from ligand C21; SER144 OG unpartnered at 4.13 ÅSwap C21 for an acceptor — no growth needed. It relieves the mismatch and can pick up SER144.
PHE140unfilled lipophilic shelfsix side-chain carbons at 4.42–7.0 Å with no ligand carbon packed against themGrow a small lipophile in: methyl→cyclopropyl, or fuse a ring onto the P1 head.
C32 terminusvector into bulk solventthe most exposed ligand atom — only 6 protein atoms within 6 ÅGrow solubility here, or cut it. Properties, not potency.

The covalent bond is not on this list: CYS145 SG is 1.81 Å from ligand C25, the anchor the reaction frame is built on rather than a degree of freedom. ASN142 carries no arrow because it is a substitution at a position the ligand already occupies, not an extension.

shared core — crystal coordinates atoms the edit adds — modelled CYS145, covalent contact gained contact lost

Each lead is one real rung-3 training row: the Change, the Intent, the Warhead decision, the contacts it Gains and Loses, and the analogue SMILES — exactly the six fields the model must produce from the pocket and the hit. The ΔpIC50 shown is illustrative only, derived from the contact ledger to make the panel readable; it is not a model output, and the measured prediction from the potency head is pending.

2Labelled dataset — g3 training examples

These are training rows, not showcase rows — five of the 2,326 in sft_out_g3, drawn from the g3_v2_input_anchored_envelope labelling pass. The third column is literally the completion the model is fine-tuned to emit: one sentence, anchored on the input crystal’s measured geometry, naming what the edit gives up and what it keeps. Every row shown carries a chair verdict of ADOPT. Orange marks the atoms that changed. Each of the five was then re-audited by three independent medicinal-chemistry reviewers against its own contact table, and all five cleared every field from all three. That audit is why these are not the rows shown earlier: of 18 candidates, 6 described their edit incorrectly and 2 cited a residue absent from their table — including three rows previously published here.

3Current results — every arm on one benchmark

Twelve trained and untrained arms, each generating against the same fixed 262-pair benchmark, copied verbatim into every arm so the rows are comparable. Cells marked TBD are not yet measured; an em-dash means the quantity does not exist for that arm — a base model that emits no sentence has no attribution rate, and scoring one would describe the parser rather than the model. Every column shares one denominator: all 262 generations. The four chemist columns and invented chemistry were previously scored only over the items an arm actually answered, which flattered arms that answer rarely — ChemDFM base read 89.6% sensible off 31 of 262 pairs. They are now multiplied by that arm’s eligibility, so a cell reads “share of all 262 pairs for which this arm produced a molecule, a sentence, and that property”, directly comparable to validity. One consequence to read carefully: invented chemistry is scaled the same way, so a low value no longer distinguishes a careful arm from a silent one — ChemDFM base and ether0 base both land on 8.4% because they rarely say anything, not because they rarely invent.

4Generation sample

Held-out test pairs — the same three pairs, three ChemDFM arms

These three pairs were chosen by blind audit, not by eye. Three medicinal-chemistry reviewers scored 12 candidate pairs across all three arms with arm identity hidden — 36 proposals, letters reshuffled per pair. These are the only three pairs every reviewer judged a fair illustration and would publish, and all three agreed on which slot is the best in each. Across the 36 proposals every cited distance was a real row of its table (36/36, all three reviewers) while only 13–19 of 36 attached it to the atom that owns it, and just 6 of 36 were judged publishable. The three pairs shown here previously were rejected unanimously.

What to look for. Orange marks the atoms that differ from the other molecule in the row. In the first pair the untrained arm hands back its own input while announcing an edit, which is what its 0.161 echo rate describes from the outside. The second pair is the uncomfortable one and is kept for that reason: all three reviewers judged the untrained arm the best slot, and it cites no distance at all while both trained arms misattribute one. The third contrasts a clean trained slot against one that makes two edits and describes a single change. Read together they say what the aggregate columns cannot: the trained arms always name a measured distance and almost never invent one, and still attach it to the wrong atom often enough that no individual attribution can be taken on trust.

ZAP70, mol1 — the ChemDFM arms

mol1 is the covalent seed, not a crystal ligand, so every distance in this prompt is predicted rather than measured: the contact table is computed from a Boltz-2 covalent cofold against ZAP70 Cys346 (ligand ipTM 0.976), 24 ligand heavy atoms against 12 pocket residues. Two consequences must travel with these rows. First, this is a distribution shift — every training row the model saw carried a table measured from a deposited crystal. Second, the pose models the warhead C–S bond at 1.40 Å against a 1.81 Å ideal, so the covalent-bond check correctly refuses to call it covalent and the row reads “unusually close, treat as uncertain” instead: mol1’s defining covalent bond never reaches the model as a covalent bond. The distance is left as the pose gives it; patching it would be fabricating geometry. These are the base, g4 and g3+g4 arms — the g3 adapter is not on the machine. Unlike section 4’s held-out pairs, these three rows have not been through a chemist panel; the attribution verdicts below are mine, checked against the generated table.

All four cited distances are real rows of the table and two of the four are attached to the wrong atom — the same extraction-works, binding-fails split measured across the whole benchmark, reproduced here on a predicted pocket. Both trained arms keep the acrylamide warhead intact, which is what a covalent programme requires. The base arm’s failure is formatting, not chemistry: it proposed acrylamide→methacrylamide, a reasonable warhead edit, and lost it to the parser.

5The three training phases

Each rung presupposes the last. Rung 1 teaches what a covalent reaction is; rung 2 teaches how to edit a molecule without breaking it; rung 3 asks for the real job — given a pocket and a covalent hit, propose a better covalent analogue and say why. A fourth channel, the potency head, spans rungs 2 and 3 and is the only part that emits a number rather than text. Each phase below is followed by its evaluation on the held-out test set, against the untuned base model and against Claude.

Phase 1 Covalent chemistry 373,935 rows · 63.9%

Four subtasks over covalent reactions, ligand-only. ADDUCT runs the reaction forward — given the electrophile and the attacking residue, write the adduct; RETRO inverts it, recovering the reactants from the product; SELECTIVITY names which residue is attacked, over six classes; WARHEAD_ID names the electrophile class, over ten. Two generative and two classification, which is the point: a model that can name a warhead but cannot form its adduct has learned vocabulary rather than chemistry, and the tables below show that gap directly. No pocket and no design decision — this rung teaches what a covalent reaction is, so the rungs above it can assume it.

Phase 1 evaluation — one table per subtask

Scored on 300 rows per subtask (1,200 generations per arm) drawn from the 32,082-row held-out fold, which is split by input molecule so no test molecule can reappear under a different subtask. Both arms get a byte-identical prompt, composed by the same function training used. For the generative subtasks, precision is the share of emitted SMILES that were correct and recall the share of asked rows answered correctly.

Phase 2 Analogue design · hit-to-lead 68,868 rows · 11.8%

Matched molecular pairs over covalent ligands. Given a hit, propose a close analogue that keeps the warhead and the binding scaffold — the two constraints that make an edit a medicinal-chemistry move rather than an arbitrary new molecule. The label names the transform before giving the SMILES, which turns open-ended generation into a decision that can be scored. Still no pocket: this rung teaches editing, not placement.

Phase 3 Covalent hit-to-lead, pocket-conditioned 3,015 unique · 2.1%

The target task, and the one shown in 3D at the top of this report. The hit arrives with its own co-crystal pocket, expressed in the covalent reaction frame: the attacked electrophilic atom at the origin, the attack axis as +z, and +x toward the Murcko-scaffold centroid. That frame is why the geometry generalises across complexes. The output is a full rationale: the structural Change, the Intent, the Warhead move, the contacts it Gains and Loses, and only then the Analogue.

Channel 4 The potency head130,667 rows · 22.3%

A Siamese MLP over [hit, analogue, analogue − hit] reading the final hidden state through a forward hook, trained with a masked regression loss so unlabelled rows contribute nothing. It predicts ΔpIC50, and it is the piece of v3 that had to be rebuilt from scratch.

Rung 3 is v5 only: v4b's rung-3 label emits a one-word class (Intent: RECOGNITION) rather than a sentence, so it has no prose to show. Rows are ordered by similarity to mol1; all eight keep the acrylamide and carry the model's own sentence. Two partial-retention patterns run in opposite directions — rows badged isoindoline held keep the warhead's ring and swap the imidazole head, while the others keep the head intact and edit the ring. Read the sentences as fluent rather than uniformly faithful: several name groups mol1 does not carry (a tosyl, a tolyl cap, a terminal aldehyde). Where a row cites pocket residues they are real — 75 of 77 citations across the cohort, 97.4%, name a residue present in the prompt — but no generation in 600 both held the scaffold and reasoned from the pocket.

ΔpIC50 is read from each arm's own Siamese potency head and is ranking-grade, not calibration-grade: on the held-out fold v4b's head scored R² −0.209 globally — worse than predicting the mean on absolute error — while reaching Spearman 0.658 within a single hit's analogue series. Comparing these 600 analogues against each other is meaningful; the absolute values are not.
